case_name: Super Sam Red Deer Ltd. v. Lethbridge (City)
text:
Alberta Court of Queen's Bench

Super Sam Red Deer Ltd. v. Lethbridge (City)

Date: 1990-08-02

T.W. Wakeling and G.D. Chipeur, for
plaintiffs.

R A. Jerke, for defendants.

(Edmonton Nos. 9006-00154; 9006-00332)

August 2, 1990. Excerpt from the transcript.

[
1
]

Agrios
J.:– The issue in this case is whether city of Lethbridge by-law
4341 requiring all retail stores over a certain size to close on Sundays is
unconstitutional because it infringes s. 2(
a
) “Freedom of Conscience and
Religion” of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The answer is “Yes”,
because the enactors of the by-law failed to make
any serious attempt to alleviate the effect of a
Sunday closing by-law on Saturday observers as called for by the Supreme Court
of Canada in
R. v. Edwards Books & Art Ltd.,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R. 713
,
55
C.R. (3d) 193
(sub nom.
R. v. Videoflicks Lt
d.
),
30 C.C.C. (3d)
385
(sub nom.
R. v. Edwards Books & Art Ltd.;
R. v. Nortown Foods Lt
d.
),
28 C.R.R. 1, 87 C.L.L.C. 14,001, 35 D.L.R. (4th) 1, 19 O.A.C. 239, 71 N.R. 161.
The by-law must accordingly be struck down.

[
2
]

The two actions were
heard together and proceeded on the basis of an agreed statement of facts, 22
exhibits entered by agreement of counsel, read-ins from the examination of
discovery of an officer of the defendant city and one of the plaintiffs.

[
3
]

All of the counsel are
to be complimented for the concise and artful presentation of the case and
arguments which permitted the real issues of the case to be considered
expeditiously by the court.

[
4
]

For the purposes of
this decision, I shall refer to but three decisions, one from the Supreme Court
of Canada, one from the British Columbia Court of Appeal, and one from the
Alberta Court of Appeal as follows:

1.
R.v. Edwards Books & Art Ltd.,

supra;

2.
Can. Safeway Ltd. v. R.,

1988 CanLII 3235 (BC CA)
, [1989] 5
W.W.R. 122, 37 B.C.L.R. (2d) 199 (C.A.);

3.
London Drugs Ltd. v. Red Deer (City),

1988 ABCA 271 (CanLII)
, 61 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1, [1988] 6 W.W.R. 173, 39 M.P.L.R. 184, 52 D.L.R. (4th)
203, 89 A.R. 173 (C.A.).

Background

[
5
]

After several months of
debate, the city council of Lethbridge passed under the provisions of
s. 241
of
the
Municipal Government Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. M-26
, by-law 4341 which, amongst
other things, required retail food stores having an area exceeding 10,000
square feet to close on Sundays and holidays. It is clear from the statement of
facts that this by-law was controversial, and council altered its position on
several occasions before concluding the by-law in its present form. The issue
remains sensitive even today.

[
6
]

The torturous history
of the by-law from mid-1989 to the present is to be found at pp. 3 to 11 of the
agreed statements of facts. It is, in turn, summarized on pp. 2 to 4 of the
plaintiff’s submissions; To present a
historic
perspective, I have summarized the highlights from these sources in App. A
attached to this amended reasons for judgment [Appendix omitted].

[
7
]

On 31st July 1989 counsel voted to ask the
electorate of the city: “Are you in favour of open Sunday shopping?” On 16th
October of that year, 12,165 voted no, 10,425 voted yes. (In percentages I am
told this is 54 per cent no, 46 per cent yes).

[
8
]

Council gave first reading to the by-law 14th
November and thereafter followed many changes after the representations of
interested parties.

[
9
]

The plaintiffs commenced action seeking a
declaration that the bylaw was void. Interim injunctions were granted by
justices of this court in February and March preventing the city from enforcing
by by-law pending judgment at the trial of this action.

[
10
]

The preamble of the by-law is set out in full in
App. B to this memorandum [Appendix omitted]. The wording is, not by
coincidence, I judge, virtually identical to the preamble of a similar by-law
in the city of Red Deer. It provides for a common pause day or a common day of
rest to enhance the quality of life and to generally promote the health and
welfare of the citizens of the city.

[
11
]

In the three authorities I have cited, the
courts have universally held that similar by-laws are secular, and where
appropriate exceptions are made, constitutional. Accepting that the by-law has
a valid purpose, the necessary analysis is whether the effect of the by-law
makes it unconstitutional.

[
12
]

The Red Deer by-law differs in one significant
feature from that of Lethbridge. It allows a retailer a completely free choice
of which day in seven one closes. The Lethbridge by-law provides no such
choice. Sunday is the pause day. In Red Deer, every affected business chooses
the day of the week in which it will close.

[
13
]

The Red Deer by-law was upheld by the Alberta
Court of Appeal. Briefly stated, the issue in this case is whether the lack of
a similar option or choice is fatal to the Lethbridge by-law. It is curious
that with the experience of the Red Deer by-law before it, the Lethbridge city
council would choose not to insert some similar exclusionary clause, but this
observation is made gratuitously and in hindsight.

[
14
]

Both corporate plaintiffs, Super Sam Red Deer
Ltd. and London Drugs Ltd., carry on business in Lethbridge, one being a retail
food store and the other a pharmacy, and the size of their square footage is
greater than that permitted by the Lethbridge by-law and would require both
plaintiffs’ stores to remain closed on Sundays.

[
15
]

From the agreed statement of facts, I set out
the following facts which are necessary for these reasons:

1. In 1989 the population of Lethbridge was
60,610.

2. Both members of the Jewish faith and the
Seventh-Day Adventist faith are Saturday observers; that is, Saturday is their
Sabbath.

3. There are 35 Jewish families in Lethbridge
and there are 150 individuals listed in the membership rolls of the Lethbridge
Seventh-Day Adventist Church.

4. There are at present no Seventh-Day Adventist
retailers in the city of Lethbridge.

Analysis

[
16
]

Most of the three days of argument before me
were devoted by counsel for the parties to a detailed analysis of the Supreme
Court of Canada decision in
Edwards Books.
As in the other decisions, I
have accepted that the by-law was passed for secular purposes and I need not
comment further on the lengthy arguments put by both counsel on that point.

[
17
]

I impute no sinister or collateral purposes to
the municipal council, and do not question the bona fides of council in what it
has done.

[
18
]

Côté J.A. stated in the Alberta Court of Appeal
decision in
London Drugs v. Red Deer (City)
that
Edwards Books
says
to test impugned legislation first for purpose, then for effect. In Red Deer,
there was no satisfactory evidence that there was a religious purpose in the
by-law. As to effect, Côté J.A. held that the by-law had no effects which were
religious or discriminatory, for every business could freely choose any day in
the seven that it will close, and they choose the day after the fact and may
change the day from week to week. Can the same be said for the effect of the Lethbridge
by-law? I think not.

[
19
]

Rather than starting afresh to re-examine
Edwards
Books,
I am satisfied that the task has already been accomplished both
thoroughly and succinctly by Seaton J.A. in the British Columbia Court of
Appeal decision of
Can. Safeway Ltd.
,
rendered in December 1988. Rather
than reinventing the judicial wheel, I shall but summarize and paraphrase
Justice Seaton’s reasons thusly.

[
20
]

The British Columbia Act starts with a general
prohibition of holiday openings. Sunday is a holiday. The purpose of the
British Columbia legislation to provide a common rest day is secular, and
therefore a valid purpose that does not violate the
Charter
.

[
21
]

When the purpose of the legislation is valid, it
is necessary to consider the impact of the legislation upon religious freedom.
The Crown, in its argument, overlooked the rights of customers and employees as
well as retailers’ rights which must be considered. Even if we only consider
retailers, the reasoning of the Crown is flawed. The agreed statement of facts
says it is a tenet of the religion of Jews and Seventh-Day Adventists that they
shall not work or transact business on Saturday, and there are people of both
faiths who live and work in Cranbrook, British Columbia. Clearly a similar
statement can be made for British Columbia generally.

[
22
]

Whether or not there are retailers who would
choose to close on Saturday and open on Sunday, I do not think it to be
decisive, for it is the
option
to which they are entitled. The effect of
this legislation is to impair their religious freedom to choose. The Act
infringes on freedom of religion. The question is whether the British Columbia
Act is a reasonable limit on the freedom of religion in considering
s. 1
of the

Charter
. In
Edwards Books,
Dickson C.J.C. summarized the effect of the
previous Supreme Court of Canada decision on s. 1 [p. 768]:

The proportionality requirement, in turn,
normally has three aspects: the limiting measures must be carefully designed,
or rationally connected, to the objective; they must impair the right as little
as possible; and their effects must not so severely trench on individual or
group rights that the legislative objective, albeit important, is nevertheless
outweighed by the abridgment of rights.

[
23
]

I accept that the first requirement is satisfied
in this case. The reasoning in
Edwards Books
leads inevitably to the
conclusion that the legislative objective is of sufficient importance to
warrant overriding a constitutional right. The Ontario legislation contained a
provision which did allow some small businesses with fewer than seven employees
and less than 5,000 square feet to open on Sunday if they closed on Saturday. That
provision gave people the option which is denied them under the British
Columbia legislation. The presence of that option, in my view, is central to
the view of Dickson C.J.C. that the second requirement was met. He said [p.
772]:

A more difficult question – and one which
goes to the heart of this litigation – is whether the
Retail Business
Holidays Act
abridges the freedom of religion of Saturday observers as
little as is reasonably possible. Section 3(4) has the effect, and was intended
to have the effect, of very substantially reducing the impact of the Act on
those religious groups for whom Saturday is a Sabbath.

[
24
]

Later, in his judgment, this is found (at p.
782):

In my view, the principles articulated in
Oakes

[
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103] make it incumbent on a legislature which enacts
Sunday closing laws to attempt very seriously to alleviate the effects of those
laws on Saturday observers. The exemption in s. 3(4) of the Act under review in
these appeals represents a satisfactory effort on the part of the Legislature
of Ontario to that end and is, accordingly, permissible.

[
25
]

He concludes on this point (at p. 783):

In view of the extent and quality of the
abridgment of rights flowing from the legislation, I have little difficulty in
applying the third element of the proportionality test. The infringement is not
disproportionate to the legislative objectives. A serious effort has been made
to accommodate the freedom of religion of Saturday observers, in so far as that
is possible without undue damage to the scope and quality of the pause day
objective. It follows that I would uphold the Act under s. 1.

[
26
]

The reasons of Dickson C.J.C. were those of the
majority of the five justices that dealt with this subject. Chouinard and Le Dain
JJ. agreed with Dickson C.J.C. Beetz and McIntyre JJ. found the Ontario
legislation did not contravene the freedoms guaranteed by s. 2(
a
) and
did not have to deal with the question.

[
27
]

Wilson J. was of the view that the exemption in
s. 3(4) did not save the legislation because it did not encompass large
retailers. Her requirement for an exemption clause was somewhat stronger than
that of the Chief Justice. La Forest J. parted with the Chief Justice in that
he had a significant difference of view regarding the Sabbatarian exemption. La
Forest J. was of the view that the Ontario Act would be valid even if it did
not contain the exemption found in s. 3(4). However, the approach of La Forest
J. was not one that we can take for he was alone in his view that the
legislation passed the constitutionality test without the exemption. So where
it is possible without injury to the legislative scheme or the rights of others
to alleviate the effects of those laws on those whose
religious freedoms are violated, such provision must
be made before it can be said that the legislation is a reasonable limit.

[
28
]

For reasons that I need
not consider in this case, Seaton J.A. held and declared the whole of the
British Columbia legislations inoperative, for to do otherwise, it would be
necessary to identify those to whom the legislation would not apply and
identify an appropriate remedy. He declined to do so and concludes that this is
not a case in which there can be a partial invalidating or constitutional
exemption, but this is one in which the legislation must be declared
inoperative.

[
29
]

That ends my summary of
Justice Seaton’s reasons taken from the
Can. Safeway
case.

[
30
]

Counsel for the
plaintiffs clearly endorse the interpretation of Justice Seaton. They argue
that the message of
Edwards Books
is that a Sunday closing by-law will
only be upheld if an accommodation is included in the law for those whose
religious observance falls on another day of the week. They further argued that
while the Supreme Court of Canada has said it is incumbent on the legislature
which enacts Sunday closing bylaws to attempt very seriously to alleviate the
effects of those laws on Saturday observers, the Lethbridge city council made
no attempt, let alone a serious attempt, to accommodate Saturday observers. I
must agree.

[
31
]

At the end of the day,
whether you call the exemption clause an accommodation or an option, Lethbridge
did not satisfy the requirement as articulated in
Edwards Books.

The defendant’s argument

[
32
]

Counsel for the city of
Lethbridge has, with considerable effort, endeavoured to distinguish this case
from that of the
Can. Safeway
decision. I consider it appropriate to
deal with some of his arguments as to whether it can be distinguished. Time has
not permitted me to respond to all of the able arguments presented by Mr. Jerke,
but I have accepted the reasoning in
Can. Safeway
and I restrict my
observations to those areas.

[
33
]

It is argued that the
size of the area covered by the by-law is a much more restricted geographical
area, that is, the city of Lethbridge has a much smaller population base than
either the entire province of British Columbia or the entire province of
Ontario. It is suggested the potential for the by-law to affect religious
freedom is greatly reduced, and the
legislation, if it
affects religious freedom at all, only creates a burden which is “trivial or
insubstantial”.

[
34
]

I am not persuaded that the mere size of the
area of population will alleviate the problem. There are Saturday observers
living in the city of Lethbridge. To suggest because their numbers are
relatively small and the city of Lethbridge has a population of about 60,000,
that these rights should be less than those of Saturday observers in British
Columbia and Ontario is not, with respect, trivial or insubstantial to those
who are affected. The answer is not to be found in their smaller numbers and
size of the community affected by the by-law.

[
35
]

In addition, it is suggested there is a further
distinction to be found based on the size of the retail store square footage
exemption. In the British Columbia Act, retail businesses of less than 225
square meters may remain open. Counsel agreed for comparison purposes this to
be about 2,500 square feet, compared to the 10,000 square feet provision in the
Lethbridge by-law. It is suggested that this was an attempt to alleviate the
effect of the law on Saturday observers. Respectfully, I cannot agree. A
serious effort to accommodate the freedom of religion of Saturday observers is
called for. This has not been accomplished merely by increasing the size of the
retail store that may remain open. This is not what was contemplated by the
Supreme Court of Canada, and in no way truly attempts to alleviate the effect
of the law on those whose religious freedoms were affected.

[
36
]

It is further suggested there is insufficient
evidence in this case to justify the conclusion that freedom of religion is
affected and that the Saturday observers are in the same position as the
Moslems, Hindus and Sikhs were in
Edwards Books.
As argued by plaintiffs’
counsel, the agreed statement of facts and the number of Saturday observers is
a complete answer to the insufficient evidence arguments. No such evidence
existed for the other religious minorities in
Edwards Books.

[
37
]

As was said in
Edwards Books,
the courts
are not called upon to substitute judicial opinion for legislative ones as to
the place at which to draw a precise line. However, in this case, the city of Lethbridge
has failed to draw any line, and this failure, as suggested by plaintiffs’
counsel, is fatal.

[
38
]

It may be unintended, but the arguments of
counsel for the defendant reflect the position of La Forest J. in
Edwards
Books,
but as was said by Seaton J.A. in
Can. Safeway Ltd.
,
the
approach of La Forest J. is not one we can take, for he was alone in his view
that the legislation passed the constitutionality test without the Sabbatarian
exemption clause. In summary, therefore, I am unable to distinguish in any
significant aspect the case at bar and the
Can. Safeway
decision. There
has been no attempt and there is no option or accommodation made in the Lethbridge
by-law for Saturday observers.

[
39
]

The legislation must accordingly be declared
inoperative.

[
40
]

Having found for the plaintiff on its principal
argument, any comment on the second and third arguments may well be academic.
If requested, I would have been inclined to adopt the arguments of counsel for
the city of Lethbridge. I did not find the definition of greenhouse to be
ambiguous or uncertain and certainly not sufficiently so to strike down the
by-law for vagueness. Nor do I see any basis that the by-law is beyond the
powers granted to the city of Lethbridge under the Municipal Government Act. If
it becomes necessary to provide further reasons on these two questions, I will
do so; however, I had undertaken to counsel to make a decision in this case
prior to the end of June and have done so by responding to the first question
presented.

[
41
]

At the end of the proceedings, I complimented
all counsel on the fairness of their research and the quality of their
advocacy. Through unusual circumstances and changes of assignments, I regret I
commenced these proceedings quite unprepared, and accordingly I put an extra
burden on all counsel. I thank them for the manner in which they introduced me
to the problems and issues, and having reviewed their arguments and my notes,
my thanks are in no way diminished. I hesitate to add that the 62 authorities
presented by plaintiffs’ counsel may not all have been required, but I was
nonetheless fascinated from a historical perspective with the annual report of
the Alberta Lord’s Day Alliance (1910-11), (1911-12). Regrettably, the
information contained therein did not play a substantial part in my decision.

[
42
]

Since the preparation of this judgment, in fact
but late yesterday, I received from the solicitors for the plaintiffs a copy of
the judgment of Southey J. of the Supreme Court of Ontario in a similar case,
Peel
(Regional Mun.) v. Great Atl. & Pac. Co. of Can.
which judgment was
released on Friday, 22nd June 1990 [reported
1990 CanLII 6850 (ON HCJ)
, 73 O.R. (2d) 289]. I have not had
an opportunity to study this judgment, except for a most hasty glance, but I
take it Southey J. takes the same views as do I of the
Edwards Books
criteria.

[
43
]

Since that decision, the Ontario legislature amended
the Retail Business Holidays Act in February 1989. A new Sabbatarian exemption
was introduced into that by-law, which is somewhat along the lines of that in
the Red Deer exception, except it provides a person may close on another day
other than Sunday, with the restriction that the closing of another day must be
by reason of the religion of the owner. Southey J. held that the new Sabbatarian
exemption reflects a reasonable trade-off and is not unconstitutional by reason
of
s. 1
of the
Charter
. However, later in the judgment, he notes that the Act
also contains a new municipal exemption which I take it permits municipalities
to, in effect, opt out of the entire –

[
44
]

Mr. Chipeur:
Law.

[
45
]

Agrios
J.: – law. There are certain provisions as to how they go about this.
He held that the effect of the new municipal exemption was an infringement on
their freedom of religion and could not be justified under the rules in
Edwards
Books
under
s. 1
of the
Charter
. He therefore struck down the entire by-law
by reason of the municipal exemption.

[
46
]

The other matters referred to by Southey J. were
not argued before me and need not be considered.

[Discussion omitted by request.]

[
47
]

Agrios
J.: Following argument as to the question of special costs for
written argument, everyone has agreed that it would be appropriate to provide
such a special award, the only question relates to quantum. In my way of
thinking, the written argument of both counsel literally shortened what could
have been a matter that would go several days, so this is a compromise figure.
I am going to award costs of $4,000 to the plaintiffs for written argument.

[
48
]

With respect to the written argument of the
injunctions, I am sorry, I do not think I am qualified to give any special
awards. I was not there, I was not present, and I do not think I can do that. I
am sorry.

[Discussion omitted by request.]

Declaration accordingly.
